contributions.statement: A tactical-recommendation retrieval layer over externalized task state is an efficiency lever, not a capability lever: budget it to cut steps/cost on tasks the agent could already solve, and measure solvable-set coverage separately, since removing it left the solvable set unchanged while cutting successful-task rounds ~33% (medium) and ~48% (hard).
contributions.evidence: §5.4 Table 3 (Intentest vs Intentest-noIntent, same system, DAG and scheduler retained): identical success set; successful-task rounds 7.2->10.8 medium, 9.4->18.3 hard. Single model (DeepSeek V4 Pro), one run, ~34-task CTF benchmark, security domain; efficiency is prior-coverage-dependent (§6.3).

contributions.statement: For long-horizon multi-repo agent runs, hold verified facts (which build passed, which contract/schema version is current) as immutable nodes in a persistent store outside the context window and gate the next action on being grounded in those facts, to curb the context-forgetting and state-confusion failures that dominate long runs.
contributions.evidence: §6.1 failure analysis: baselines fail via premature-success (F1), host/role-state confusion (F2), missed signals in long output (F3). §6.2 triangulation of noIntent ablation + VulnBot contrast (44.1% vs 88.2%) + failure patterns. Authors call this 'corroborating rather than conclusive'; the DAG itself is never ablated (§7), so the solvability attribution is cross-system and confounded.
relative_to: P36 static workflow graph / state machine

reason: One contribution qualifies: the cleanly-ablated finding that the retrieval layer buys efficiency, not new solvable tasks, which a Java lead can act on when scoping a 'next-step' layer over repo memory. The persistent-fact-state design pattern stays weak because the graph's solvability benefit is only cross-system/structural, never isolated (authors concede the DAG cannot be ablated). The headline injection-defense and 88.2% success claims are domain-specific and confounded, so they do not back a gate.
